analogy.p: Think of ultrasound like shouting 'hello' across a canyon and timing how long it takes for the echo to come back. If the echo returns after 2 seconds, the sound has gone to the cliff and back, so the cliff is only 1 second of sound travel away (about 330 m), which is why we halve the time. A medical probe does the same but with a pulse so short and high-pitched that it can map the tiny boundaries between tissues, and a computer plays the role of your brain, turning the timings into a picture. The analogy breaks down because a shout spreads out in all directions and is partly absorbed, whereas an ultrasound beam is narrow and carefully directed, and only part of it is reflected at each boundary.

bullets: Sound is a **longitudinal wave**: the particles vibrate **parallel** to the direction the wave travels, producing **compressions and rarefactions**.
Sound needs a **medium**; it **cannot travel through a vacuum** because there are no particles to vibrate.
**Human hearing range:** about **20 Hz to 20 000 Hz** (20 kHz).
**Ultrasound:** frequencies **above 20 000 Hz**; **infrasound** is below 20 Hz.
Ultrasound is **partially reflected** when it meets a boundary between two media, and the reflection time is used to find distances.
Uses: **foetal scans, other medical imaging, industrial flaw detection, sonar**.
Equations you may need: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)**, **distance (m) = speed (m/s) × time (s)**.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8463 (Waves) expects you to know that **sound waves are longitudinal**, that they travel through a medium by making its particles vibrate, and that the **human ear can hear frequencies from about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz (20 kHz)**. You must also know that **ultrasound** is sound with a **frequency higher than 20 000 Hz**, that it is **partially reflected at boundaries between two different media**, and that measuring the **time for echoes to return** lets you work out distances. This gives uses in **medical imaging, industrial imaging (flaw detection) and sonar/echo sounding**. Higher tier candidates must also explain how sound is converted to vibrations in the ear and why this limits the range of human hearing.

bullets: **Compression:** a region where particles are closer together than normal; air pressure is **higher**.
**Rarefaction:** a region where particles are further apart than normal; air pressure is **lower**.
**Wavelength:** the distance from one compression to the next compression (or rarefaction to rarefaction).
**Frequency:** the number of waves (compressions) passing a point each second, measured in **hertz (Hz)**; it determines the **pitch** of the sound.
**Amplitude:** the maximum displacement of the particles (or the size of the pressure variation); it determines the **loudness** or volume.
A **high-pitched** sound has a **high frequency** (short wavelength); a **loud** sound has a **large amplitude**.
The wave transfers **energy** from the source to the detector without transferring matter along the wave.
Because sound needs particles, it **cannot travel through a vacuum** (unlike electromagnetic waves).
core.p: When a source such as a loudspeaker cone vibrates, it pushes on the nearby air particles, squashing them together to make a **compression** (a region of higher pressure), then moves back, leaving a **rarefaction** (a region of lower pressure) where the particles are spread out. These regions pass along the air as the wave travels, but the **particles themselves only vibrate back and forth about fixed positions**: the wave transfers **energy** and **information**, not matter. Because the vibrations are in the same direction as the wave travels, sound is a **longitudinal** wave, unlike water ripples or light, which are transverse.

bullets: Speed in air ≈ **330 m/s** (quote 330 m/s unless the question gives another value).
Speed in water ≈ **1500 m/s**; in solids it is typically several thousand m/s.
**Why faster in solids:** particles are **closer together** and held in a rigid structure, so vibrations are **passed on more quickly**.
When sound passes from air to water or a solid, its **speed and wavelength increase** but its **frequency stays the same** (determined by the source).
Use **v = f × λ**: if v increases and f is constant, then λ must increase.
The speed of sound in air does not depend on the loudness or the pitch of the sound.
Higher temperature gives faster particles and a (slightly) higher speed of sound in air.
Sound can be **reflected (echoes)**, **absorbed** and **refracted**, as other waves can.
core.h: Speed of sound in different materials
core.p: Sound travels as vibrations passing from particle to particle, so the speed depends on how quickly the particles can pass vibrations on to each other. In **solids** the particles are close together and strongly bonded, so vibrations are passed on very quickly; in **liquids** they are close but less strongly held; in **gases** particles are far apart, so there are fewer collisions and the vibration passes on slowly. This gives the order of speeds: **solids > liquids > gases**. A typical speed of sound in air is about **330 m/s** (around 340 m/s at room temperature); in water it is about **1500 m/s**; in steel about 5000 m/s.

bullets: v = f × λ; rearranged: **f = v ÷ λ** and **λ = v ÷ f**.
Example: a 500 Hz note in air (330 m/s): λ = 330 ÷ 500 = **0.66 m**.
Convert units first: **1 kHz = 1000 Hz**, **1 MHz = 1 000 000 Hz**, **1 cm = 0.01 m**.
Medical ultrasound often uses **1 MHz to 15 MHz**; at 2.0 MHz in tissue (1500 m/s) λ = 1500 ÷ 2 000 000 = **7.5 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.75 mm**.
A shorter wavelength can **resolve smaller details**, so higher-frequency ultrasound gives a sharper picture but is absorbed more and penetrates less deeply.
The **period** T = 1 ÷ f gives the time for one complete wave.
Use **distance = speed × time** for echoes and thunder: sound takes about **3 seconds to travel 1 km** in air.
core.h: The wave equation applied to sound
core.p: The **wave speed equation** applies to every wave: **wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) × wavelength (m)**, written v = f λ. This allows you to find the wavelength of any sound from its frequency and the speed of sound in the medium. Because audible frequencies range from 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, in air (330 m/s) the wavelengths range from about **16.5 m** down to about **1.65 cm**. Ultrasound has even shorter wavelengths, which is important because **short wavelengths can reveal small details** and are reflected from small features.

bullets: **Step 1:** sound waves travel through the air as longitudinal pressure waves and reach the **ear drum**.
**Step 2:** the pressure variations make the **ear drum vibrate** at the same frequency as the sound.
**Step 3:** the vibrations are passed on through **other parts of the ear** (small bones and the cochlea), which are solid/fluid structures.
**Step 4:** nerve cells convert the vibrations to **electrical impulses** which travel to the brain.
**Why limited range:** the ear's structures can vibrate **efficiently only over a limited range of frequencies**, so frequencies above about 20 kHz or below about 20 Hz are not detected.
Hearing range **decreases with age** and with exposure to loud noise; the upper limit often falls well below 20 kHz.
Sound travelling through solids causes the solid to **vibrate**; this is why you can feel bass through a floor.
Different animals have different hearing ranges; dogs and bats can detect **ultrasound** that humans cannot.
core.h: Hearing: how the ear detects sound (Higher tier)
core.p: Sound waves in air reach the ear and make the **eardrum** vibrate. These vibrations are passed through **other parts of the ear** (small bones, then the fluid-filled cochlea) which convert them into **electrical signals** sent along the nerve to the brain, which we experience as sound. The **conversion of sound waves to vibrations of solids** (and of the fluid in the cochlea) only works **over a limited frequency range**, which is why humans cannot hear below about 20 Hz or above about 20 000 Hz. Higher tier questions ask you to **explain the limits of human hearing** using this idea.

bullets: Ultrasound: **frequency > 20 000 Hz**.
Produced by **electrical circuits** that make oscillations over a wide range of frequencies; these can drive a transducer to produce sound with the **same frequency** as the electrical oscillation.
Ultrasound is **partially reflected** at the boundary between two different media (some is transmitted, some reflected).
The **time taken** for the reflected waves to return to a detector allows the **distance to the boundary** to be calculated.
It is **non-ionising** and generally **safe for imaging soft tissue** and unborn babies, unlike X-rays.
Because ultrasound has a **short wavelength**, it can produce detailed images and be directed in a narrow beam.
Ultrasound is **absorbed** by tissue and loses intensity with depth; higher frequencies are absorbed more quickly.
In scans a **gel** is applied between the probe and skin to remove air, because air would reflect most of the ultrasound at the skin surface.
core.p: **Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency **higher than 20 000 Hz**, above the range of human hearing. It is produced when **electrical oscillations** of the right frequency are applied to a transducer (such as a crystal), which vibrates at the same frequency and makes sound waves with the same frequency as the electrical oscillation. A detector then converts the returning ultrasound back into electrical signals. Because we cannot hear ultrasound, it can be used safely and silently, and unlike X-rays it is **non-ionising**, so it does not damage cells in the way ionising radiation can.

bullets: Distance travelled by the pulse = **speed × time**.
Distance to the boundary **d = (v × t) ÷ 2**, since the pulse travels there and back.
Typical speed of ultrasound in soft tissue ≈ **1500 m/s**; in water ≈ **1500 m/s**.
Example: an echo returns after **80 μs (8.0 × 10⁻⁵ s)** in tissue: d = 1500 × 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ ÷ 2 = **0.060 m = 6.0 cm**.
Multiple boundaries give **multiple echoes** at different times, so the depths of several layers can be found.
The greater the **difference between the media** (e.g. tissue and bone), the **larger the proportion reflected**.
A computer uses the **time delays** and **strengths** of echoes to **build an image**.
If a question gives the **total time** for the echo, remember to **halve** it, or halve the distance; this is the most common mistake.
core.h: Partial reflection at boundaries and echo ranging
core.p: When ultrasound reaches the boundary between two media (for example between muscle and bone, or between water and the sea bed), **some of the wave is reflected and some is transmitted**; this is **partial reflection**. The reflected wave, an **echo**, returns to a detector next to the source. Because the speed of the wave in the medium is known, the **distance to the boundary** can be worked out from the time delay between sending the pulse and detecting the echo. The pulse goes to the boundary **and back**, so the total distance travelled is **twice** the distance to the boundary, which is why you must **divide by 2**.

bullets: **Foetal scanning:** ultrasound is sent into the abdomen; echoes from the foetus are used to form an image to check **growth and development**.
**Other medical imaging:** heart (echocardiograms), liver, kidneys, muscles, and blood flow.
**Advantages:** **non-ionising**, so not damaging to cells; **painless** and **non-invasive**; **real-time** images; relatively **cheap** and portable.
**Limitations:** poorer images through **bone and gas** (air in the lungs or bowel reflects almost all of the ultrasound).
A **gel** is applied between the skin and probe to **remove the air gap**, so more ultrasound enters the body.
The images are lower quality than **CT or MRI**, but ultrasound is far safer and quicker.
**Ultrasound therapy** can break up kidney stones (a different use: high-intensity waves cause the stones to break into small pieces that pass out naturally).
Typical frequencies used for medical imaging are in the range **1 MHz to 15 MHz**.
core.p: The best-known medical use is **prenatal scanning** of a foetus. A probe containing a transmitter and detector is moved over the skin, sending short pulses of ultrasound into the body. Echoes are reflected from boundaries between tissues, such as the boundary between amniotic fluid and the foetus's skin, and a computer builds up an **image** from the times and strengths of the echoes. Ultrasound is also used to look at organs such as the heart, liver and kidneys, and to examine muscles and tendons. It is preferred to X-rays for this purpose because it is **non-ionising** and **does not harm the unborn baby**.

bullets: **Industrial flaw detection:** an echo that arrives sooner than expected shows a **boundary inside the material**, such as a crack.
It is a **non-destructive test**, so the part can still be used afterwards.
**Sonar:** a ship sends out a pulse and measures the **time** for the echo from the sea bed or an object.
**Depth = (speed in water × time) ÷ 2**; the speed of sound in sea water is about **1500 m/s**.
Sonar can detect **fish shoals, wrecks and submarines**, and is used to make **maps of the sea bed**.
Other uses of echo ranging: **bats and dolphins** use echolocation to find prey and navigate.
Compare with **seismic waves** which also use reflections at boundaries to study the structure of the Earth.
Ultrasound is also used for **cleaning** delicate objects such as jewellery; vibrations shake dirt off the surface (not required detail for exam).
core.p: Ultrasound is also used to find **hidden flaws** in materials such as metal pipes, aircraft parts and railway lines. A probe sends ultrasound into the object; if there is a **crack or air gap** inside, a partial reflection comes back from it **earlier** than the echo from the far side, so the flaw can be detected and its depth found without damaging the object. **Sonar** (sound navigation and ranging) uses ultrasound or sound pulses sent from a ship to measure the **depth of the sea** or to find shoals of fish, wrecks and submarines. The time delay between sending the pulse and receiving the echo from the sea bed gives the depth.

bullets: **Echo:** the reflection of sound from a hard surface, heard after a time delay.
Sound is reflected according to the **law of reflection** (angle of incidence = angle of reflection).
**Soft materials** (foam, curtains, carpet) **absorb** sound; **hard smooth** materials reflect it.
To hear a separate echo the delay must be about **0.1 s** or more, so the surface must be at least **17 m** away in air (330 m/s × 0.1 s ÷ 2).
Example: a person hears an echo **2.0 s** after shouting; distance = 330 × 2.0 ÷ 2 = **330 m**.
**Thunder** is heard after lightning because light travels almost instantly but sound travels at about 330 m/s.
Echoes can be used to **measure the speed of sound** by timing the echo from a wall at a known distance.
Link to other topics: the same ideas are used for **radar and seismic reflections**.
core.h: Reflection, absorption and echoes of sound
core.p: Sound waves are **reflected** from hard, smooth surfaces and give **echoes** if the reflecting surface is far enough away (at least about 17 m) for the reflected sound to be heard as a separate sound. Soft, rough materials such as curtains and carpets **absorb** sound, which reduces echoes. Sound that reflects from many surfaces close together causes **reverberation**, a prolonged sound, which is why large empty halls have a lot of echo. Understanding this is the basis of echo ranging, and of the design of concert halls and recording studios.

bullets: **Frequency** is determined by the **source** and does not change when the wave enters another medium.
**Speed and wavelength** change when the medium changes, and increase together if the wave speeds up.
Example: a 2000 Hz sound has λ = 330 ÷ 2000 = **0.165 m** in air and λ = 1500 ÷ 2000 = **0.75 m** in water.
The more different two media are, the greater the proportion of ultrasound reflected at their boundary.
Air–skin boundary reflects **almost all** ultrasound, hence the gel.
Sound can also be **refracted** when it enters a medium at an angle because its speed changes.
Sound that travels through **solids** makes the solid vibrate; this transfers energy and is detected by microphones in some devices.
Compare **transverse** (light, ripples) and **longitudinal** (sound) waves: only transverse waves can be polarised.
core.h: Waves in different media: transmission, frequency and wavelength
core.p: When sound passes from one medium into another, such as air into water, **some is reflected and some is transmitted**. The **frequency stays the same** because it is set by the source, but the **speed changes**, so the **wavelength changes** (v = f λ). Because the speed in water or in a solid is much greater than in air, the wavelength is much longer for the same frequency. This is why ultrasound is hard to get from air into the body without a gel: the two media are very different, so most of the energy is reflected at the boundary.

bullets: Always check the **units**: seconds, metres, hertz; convert μs, ms, kHz and MHz.
For **echo questions**: d = v × t ÷ 2 (the factor of 2 is almost always tested).
From an **oscilloscope trace**: period T = number of divisions × time base; frequency f = 1 ÷ T.
On a **waveform graph**, amplitude is the maximum displacement from the middle; wavelength is the distance between peaks.
In a **scan diagram**, a larger echo gives a stronger reflection; the delay between pulse and echo gives distance.
Check the answer is **sensible**: ocean depth of hundreds of metres, tissue depth of centimetres.
**Compare and contrast** questions: longitudinal vs transverse; audible vs ultrasound; X-rays vs ultrasound.
Use words from the mark scheme: **'partially reflected at the boundary'**, **'time taken for the echo to return'**, **'distance = speed × time'**.
core.h: Data, graphs and exam skills for sound and ultrasound
core.p: Typical exam questions for this topic give you a time and a speed and ask for a distance, or give a diagram of echoes from a scan or an oscilloscope trace. You need to be systematic: write the equation, substitute with correct units, remember the factor of 2 for echoes, and give a sensible number of significant figures. For oscilloscope traces, read the **time base** (time per division) to convert horizontal distance into time, then use it to work out the frequency or the echo delay.

exam: **State (1 mark):** 'sound is a longitudinal wave'; 'ultrasound has a frequency above 20 000 Hz'; 'human hearing range is 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz'.
**Describe a longitudinal wave (2 marks):** 'the vibrations/oscillations are parallel to the direction of energy transfer', and 'there are compressions and rarefactions'.
**Calculation of distance by echo (3 marks):** write d = v × t ÷ 2; substitute; give answer with units (e.g. 1500 × 0.80 ÷ 2 = 600 m). Marks are often lost by forgetting to divide by 2.
**Wave equation (3 marks):** v = f × λ; rearrange for the quantity needed; convert kHz/MHz to Hz first.

**Explain how ultrasound is used in a scan (4 marks):** 'pulses sent into the body', 'partially reflected at boundaries between different tissues', 'time for echoes to return is measured', 'the computer uses the times to determine distances and produce an image'.
**Explain why gel is used (2 marks):** 'removes air between probe and skin'; 'air would reflect most of the ultrasound, so more enters the body'.
**Compare ultrasound and X-rays (2 to 3 marks):** ultrasound is non-ionising so safer, but X-rays show bone and give better detail through bone.

**Higher tier ear question (3 marks):** 'sound waves make the ear drum vibrate', 'vibrations are passed through the ear and converted into electrical signals', 'this only works over a limited frequency range so limits hearing'.
**Explain why sound is faster in solids (2 marks):** 'particles are closer together', 'so vibrations pass between particles more quickly'.
**Graph/trace tips:** use the time base to find time; amplitude is measured from the centre line, not peak to trough; label axes with units.

mistakes.r: Sound is a longitudinal wave: particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel.
Sound travels fastest in solids because the particles are closer together and pass vibrations on more quickly.
mistakes.w: Sound travels fastest in air because the particles can move freely.

mistakes.r: The pulse travels there and back, so distance to the boundary = speed × time ÷ 2.
mistakes.w: Distance = speed × time for an echo.

mistakes.r: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency above 20 000 Hz; it is not related to loudness.
Ultrasound is non-ionising and does not damage cells in the way ionising radiation does.
mistakes.w: Ultrasound is ionising and can harm a foetus like X-rays.

mistakes.r: Frequency stays the same; the speed and wavelength change.
mistakes.w: The frequency of sound changes when it enters water.

mistakes.r: Particles only vibrate about a fixed position; energy is transferred, not matter.
mistakes.w: The particles travel along with the sound wave from the source to the ear.

mistakes.r: Sound needs particles (a medium) and cannot travel through a vacuum.
mistakes.w: Sound can travel through a vacuum if loud enough.

mistakes.r: Ultrasound is partially reflected: some reflected, some transmitted.
mistakes.w: Ultrasound is completely reflected at a boundary.

mistakes.r: Loudness depends on amplitude; pitch depends on frequency.
mistakes.w: Loudness depends on the frequency of the sound.

summary: AQA 8463: know that sound waves are longitudinal, that human hearing spans about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, and that ultrasound (above 20 000 Hz) is partially reflected at boundaries so the time for echoes to return gives distances. You must use these ideas for medical and industrial imaging and sonar, and (Higher tier) explain how the ear converts sound to vibrations and why that limits hearing. It matters because echo calculations and explanations are common Paper 2 questions.

terms.d: A wave in which the oscillations (vibrations) are parallel to the direction of energy transfer.
A region in a longitudinal wave where the particles are closer together than normal (higher pressure).
A region in a longitudinal wave where the particles are further apart than normal (lower pressure).
The number of waves passing a point each second, measured in hertz (Hz).
The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the adjacent wave.
The maximum displacement of a point on a wave away from its undisturbed position.
The speed at which energy is transferred (or the wave moves) through a medium; v = f × λ.
Sound waves with a frequency higher than 20 000 Hz, above the upper limit of human hearing.
Sound waves with a frequency lower than 20 Hz.
A reflection of a sound wave from a surface, heard (or detected) after a time delay.
When some of a wave is reflected and some is transmitted at a boundary between two media.
The material through which a wave travels.
A system that uses pulses of sound (ultrasound) and the time for echoes to return to find the distance to objects or the sea bed.
A device that converts electrical oscillations to sound waves, or sound waves to electrical signals.
How high or low a sound is; it depends on the frequency.
The unit of frequency; 1 Hz is one wave per second.
Radiation or waves that do not have enough energy to remove electrons from atoms, so do not damage cells in that way.
Using the time delay between sending a pulse and receiving the echo to measure distance.

worked.q: A ship sends a pulse of ultrasound towards the sea bed. The echo is detected 0.80 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the sea. (3 marks)
steps: Total distance travelled by the pulse = speed × time = 1500 × 0.80 = 1200 m.
This is the journey down and back, so depth = 1200 ÷ 2 = 600 m.

worked.q: Ultrasound of frequency 2.0 MHz travels through soft tissue at 1500 m/s. (a) Calculate the wavelength. (b) An echo from a boundary returns after 8.0 × 10⁻⁵ s. Calculate the depth of the boundary. (5 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: A probe produces pulses of ultrasound (frequency above 20 000 Hz) which travel into the body. At each boundary between different tissues the ultrasound is partially reflected. The detector measures the time taken for each echo to return, and since the speed is known, the computer calculates the distance to each boundary and builds up an image. Ultrasound is used because it is non-ionising, so is safe for the baby.
worked.q: Explain how ultrasound is used to produce an image of an unborn baby. (4 marks)
steps: Probe sends pulses of ultrasound into the body.
Ultrasound is partially reflected at the boundaries between different tissues.
The time taken for the echoes to return is measured by the detector.
A computer uses the times (and strength) of the echoes to work out distances and build up an image.
